title: The First mRNA Flu Shot Is Here — but the CDC Hasn't Recommended It
excerpt: The FDA approved mFLUSIVA in August, the first mRNA flu vaccine, for adults 50 and older. The CDC's guidance does not mention it; the Pentagon barred it for troops.
content:
The first flu vaccine made with mRNA technology is on the U.S. market this season — but if you ask the federal government whether you should get it, you will get two different answers, depending on who you ask.

The Food and Drug Administration approved mFLUSIVA, made by Moderna, on August 5, 2026, for adults age 50 and older. It is the first mRNA influenza vaccine ever approved in the United States. For ages 50 to 64, the FDA gave full approval. For ages 65 and older, the approval is "accelerated" — based on immune-response data rather than a trial showing the vaccine prevents flu illness in that age group — and Moderna must run another study to confirm it protects older adults from illness.

In a trial of about 40,000 adults ages 50 and older across 11 countries, mFLUSIVA reduced the risk of getting the flu by 26.6 percent compared with a standard-dose flu shot, according to results published in the New England Journal of Medicine in May 2026.

The CDC has not weighed in

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has never issued a recommendation specific to mFLUSIVA. Its September 1 guidance for the 2026–27 season does not mention the vaccine at all. The CDC's vaccine advisory committee, ACIP, has not met since a federal court froze its membership in March 2026, and its meetings for March, June and October were all canceled. The next scheduled dates are February 24–26, 2027.

The American Academy of Family Physicians, by contrast, lists mFLUSIVA as one of four preferred options for adults 65 and older, based on the trial evidence. And the Pentagon has gone the other way: it barred the shot for military personnel, including TRICARE, with an October 13 order stating the mRNA flu vaccine "is not authorized for use by any Department of War or military entity."

The vaccine is not approved for people under 50, and it is not approved for use during pregnancy because of a lack of data.

Flu season is already here

The confusion lands in the middle of a flu season that is already moving. The CDC's FluView report for the week ending November 7 said flu activity was still increasing in many parts of the country and was higher than usual for this time of year. The CDC estimates at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations and 2,100 deaths so far this season, with five pediatric deaths reported.

Webb Watch 956 is not giving medical advice. What the record shows is a new vaccine option, a federal approval, and a federal recommendation process that has stalled in court — leaving doctors, pharmacists and patients to sort it out themselves. If you are 50 or older and wondering which flu shot fits you, ask your doctor or pharmacist — and ask them what the CDC's silence means for your choice.
